references.text: The parallel text in [ref:Matt 19:14-15|Matthew 19:14-15], where Jesus says, "Let the little children come to me and do not hinder them, for the kingdom of heaven belongs to such as these", and then lays his hands on them.

The parallel text in [ref:Mark 10:14-16|Mark 10:14-16], where Jesus becomes indignant and says, "Let the little children come to me and do not hinder them, for the kingdom of God belongs to such as these", and takes them in his arms and blesses them.

In [ref:Matt 18:3-4|Matthew 18:3-4], Jesus says that one must turn around and become like a child to enter the kingdom of heaven. Whoever humbles themselves like a child is the greatest in the kingdom of heaven. This elaborates on what it means that the kingdom of God belongs to children.

In [ref:Matt 5:3|Matthew 5:3], Jesus says, "Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven." The humility and dependence of children reflect the spiritual poverty that characterizes those who belong to the kingdom of God.

In [ref:1 Kor 14:20|1 Corinthians 14:20], Paul urges believers not to be children in understanding, but to be children in evil. A childlike innocence and trust is what Jesus points to as a characteristic of those who belong to the kingdom of God.

In [ref:1 Pet 2:2|1 Peter 2:2], believers are urged to long like newborn babies for pure spiritual milk, so that by it they may grow up into salvation—a childlike hunger and dependence that aligns with Jesus' words about children's place in the kingdom of God.

In [ref:Luk 9:47-48|Luke 9:47-48], Jesus places a child beside him and says that whoever receives this child in his name receives him. This underscores the value Jesus places on children and humility.
In [ref:Mark 9:36-37|Mark 9:36-37], Jesus takes a child in his arms and says that whoever receives such a child in his name receives him. To receive the small and humble is to receive Jesus himself.

In [ref:Joh 3:3-5|John 3:3-5], Jesus tells Nicodemus that no one can see the kingdom of God unless they are born again. Becoming like a child—receiving the kingdom of God with childlike trust—is closely connected to the new birth required to enter the kingdom.
